### Executive Signal
- Agent benchmarking and learning theory dominate this cycle; **SPEEDRUNBENCH** narrows the long-horizon evaluation gap for [LLM agents](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-948dd4c2f784), while **[Singular Learning Theory](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-cbd7f86b45af)** tutorials deepen the theoretical foundation for model generalization.

### Priority Developments
- **SPEEDRUNBENCH** introduces a video-game speedrunning benchmark testing [LLM agents](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-948dd4c2f784) on long-horizon exploration and optimization, providing a new empirical yardstick for agentic capability.
- The [Singular Learning Theory](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-cbd7f86b45af) series advances Bayesian foundations with practical relevance to deep-network generalization and loss-surface analysis.
- Philosophical essays (**[Intent vs Impact](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-d16809253ebe)**, **[Low-Background Minds](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-543e4dd1889a)**) attempt agent-foundations and alignment metaphors, signaling continued theoretical maturation despite acknowledged gaps.
- [AI safety](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-bebd66b854a5) governance gains traction through bootcamps for legal practitioners and reframed [extinction](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-ed59c1fd060a) communication, shifting from binary x-risk debates toward tested messaging.
- Safety-fiction pieces and [personal methodological experiments](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-3ec39689a850) illustrate how the AI [safety](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-f9a0f06f83bc) community uses narrative and self-reflection to explore alignment and research practice.

### Leadership Implications
- Adopt agent benchmarks like **[SPEEDRUNBENCH](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-948dd4c2f784)** into capability assessment pipelines to track long-horizon planning beyond static QA.
- Invest in safety-research talent development and [tested communication strategies](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-ed59c1fd060a) to convert [governance](/?date=2026-10-04&category=research#item-bebd66b854a5) engagement into measurable alignment outcomes.

items.title: SPEEDRUNBENCH: Challenging LLM Agents With Video Game Speedrunning
items.content: SPEEDRUNBENCH tests whether agents can find faster routes across nine games. Agents play from screenshots or edit complete action traces, starting from a supplied route or from scratch. In a controlled SuperTux test, DeepSeek-V4-Pro reduced its route from 9,428 to 1,847 frames with up to 200 candidate evaluations per turn. No agent reached a human record under the practical budget.
items.author: Yoshinari Fujinuma, Keisuke Kamahori, Ryuto Koike, Abdelrahman Madkour, Varun Prashant Gangal, Monty Bichouna, Martyna Markiewicz, Shivani Jain, Duncan Curtis, Rebecca Qian, Anand Kannappan
items.summary: SPEEDRUNBENCH is a new benchmark that tests LLM agents on finding faster routes across nine video games using either screenshot inputs or direct action-trace edits, with both scratch-start and supplied-route conditions. In a controlled SuperTux experiment, DeepSeek-V4-Pro (released April 2026) shrank a route from 9,428 to 1,847 frames, but no agent matched human records within practical compute budgets. The work highlights a gap between raw agent capability and human-level route optimization in long-horizon planning.
items.reasoning: Novel agent benchmark with an interesting task design (speedrunning requires both exploration and route compression), and it provides concrete evidence that current top-tier models like DeepSeek-V4-Pro still trail human experts. Importance is moderated by the limited scale (nine games, small controlled test) and lack of a major-lab affiliation.

items.summary: The third installment in a tutorial series on Singular Learning Theory (SLT), focusing on the regular case where the true distribution is regular for the model. items.title: Intent vs Impact vs Expectation and Alternatives
items.content: I have seen plenty of discourse and writing on the subject of intent vs impact when actions lead to harm, particularly in existing interpersonal relationships. The thrust tends to be that it's unreasonable to focus the discussion or conclusions on the intent of the actor rather than the impact the actions had on the other party. Given just those two factors, I tend to agree; the intent of the actor will usually not be nearly as important or worthy of focus. I have also observed that when someone has been harmed, mentioning intent to them is rarely a useful or healthy way for the conversation to proceed.However, in my experience, those are rarely the only two factors. Often, when I hear an actor talking about "intent", it's a proxy for one or two other concepts that they might not be as capable of perceiving or discussing. When I hear the harmed party talking about "intent", it often indicates they aren't even aware of the other factors. I try to bring those concepts to the forefront when I'm involved in those discussions, regardless of whether I am the actor or the harmed or a third party.The first is the actor's reasonable expectation of the outcome of their actions. "Helping you was the reasonably predictable most likely outcome" is a much stronger argument than just "I intended to help you". For example, you should catch, or otherwise attempt to help, people falling down from ladders. It is reasonable to predict and expect that the outcome will be a significant reduction in harm. If someone says that you hurt instead of helped, and tries to dismiss your intent to help them, they missed the bigger picture. You didn't just intend to help them, you reasonably and confidently predicted that result. If you find out afterward that the actual impact was to ruin their short film stunt, that is not particularly useful information. Except to not catch that specific person again in that specific location on that specific day, your future behavior should generally not change...
items.author: sparr
items.summary: A long essay attempting to build a unified semantic framework ('Semantic Ladder') bridging rocks (sensory inputs), rules (formal languages), and meaning, drawing on Gärdenfors, Tarski, Gentner, and later Mohist philosophy. The author flags it as a half-built conceptual tower, mixing confident results with suggestive speculation, and acknowledges the lack of formal mathematics.
items.reasoning: Ambitious attempt at agent foundations / philosophy-of-language synthesis with acknowledged gaps; the topics (grounding, reference, compositionality) are core to alignment and interpretability. Speculative status limits credit.

items.title: Low-Background Minds
items.content: Opus 5.5 is a really good writer.I had a conversation about some stuff related to how hospitals work, and some vague hunches I had about AI alignment ideas, and Duncan's new "deer in the subway" post, then I asked it to write an essay and it wrote this. I think it's really good so I'm posting it.(Big Keenan fans might note that this is squarely within the "embedded agency playgrounds" research program, especially once you make the jump to, like, giving an agent autonomous control over its own "skin" or "blood-brain barrier" or whatever.)Low-Background MindsI. The red lineWalk into a hospital and nobody stops you. The lobby belongs to everyone: the coffee cart, the gift shop, the man asleep in the third row of chairs.Keep walking and things change. A door with a badge reader. A red line on the floor. Past it, scrubs and hair covers. Past the next door, masks. And at the center, the sterile field: a few square feet of draped cloth around an open wound, where only gloved hands go, only between waist and chest, and never with your back turned.None of this is a wall. It is a gradient. Each layer catches what the last one missed. Even the air is conscripted: the operating room is kept at positive pressure, so when a door swings open, air rushes out, never in. The building has a preferred direction for contamination, and it points away from the patient.We did not design this from first principles. We learned it from corpses, one infection at a time, starting with a Hungarian obstetrician in the 1840s who noticed that doctors coming from the morgue were killing mothers, and was ridiculed for saying so.II. The naked mindNow look at a language model. It has three zones, and almost nothing between them.The weights are the brain, maximally inside. While the model is running, the wall around them is absolute: nothing goes in, and only sampled tokens come out. But while the model is learning, that wall becomes a sieve with no preferences. Every gradient can reach every parameter,...

items.title: What I learnt co-leading an AI Safety bootcamp for legal and governance practitioners
items.content: AI safety has gone mainstream. More people than ever want to work on AI safety research, and there are real policy wins in the US, the UK and Europe. But political will and market incentives are now the bottleneck, and policy officers can't own correct implementation alone.Having built a Responsible AI program at an Accenture joint venture, I know profit-driven companies are hard to steer, but also that people inside them can shift practice in ways that compound: tighter contractual clauses, more scrutiny of vendors and suppliers, fewer ways for providers to get away with non-compliance. The EU has no native frontier labs, but it is a huge market (with a regulatory body that has an AI safety unit!),That leverage only works if the professionals implementing AI safety legislation, and drafting the legal mechanisms behind it, understand the technical picture: how to read the research, and where safety promises break down. The market should be choosing not the most capable models, but the partners with the strongest incentives towards safety, and only a community with this knowledge can spread that.Earlier in September, ML4Good, in partnership with EquiStamp, ran the first European Seminar on Frontier AI and Law: an intensive five-day residential bootcamp in East Sussex for 19 senior legal, governance and risk professionals from 12 jurisdictions. [1]It took participants through the full frontier AI pipeline, from training and evaluations to agents and safeguards. Each stage was tied to the questions they face in their own work: procurement, risk assessment, and where vendors' safety claims break down.What made this bootcamp different from potentially from similar AI safety fellowships, was the audience we brought together [2] . We were specifically targeting experienced professionals who are already responsible for legal, compliance, risk, and responsible AI functions within their organisations, and with little to no previous exposure to AI Safety events or EA.The cohor...

items.summary: Reflection on co-leading the first European AI safety bootcamp for legal and governance practitioners, run by ML4Good with EquiStamp in September. The author argues that legislative traction in the EU now outpaces technical understanding among implementers, and that practitioners need real fluency in safety research to push procurement and contracts toward safer providers.

items.title: You can't use it without becoming like me
items.content: A Ukrainian fibre-optic drone — copied from Russians. (АрміяІнформ, CC-BY 4.0)Mick Ryan describes the fast following loop in war. Ukraine pioneered mobile teams to hunt drones. Russia copied it and incorporated it into its own defense. Russia came with unjammable fibre-optic drones but Ukraine quickly followed. After Ukraine developed uncrewed naval drones, Russia built its own.The wheel of action and counteraction turns ever faster:The most consequential fast following, though, has been institutional. Ukraine built the world’s first Unmanned Systems Forces branch in 2024. Russia’s Rubicon Center was established as a response to Ukrainian drone innovation and in November 2025 Moscow stood up its own Unmanned Systems Forces. Fast following has moved from copying a weapon to copying tactics to copying an entire force structure.Extend that logic further, and eventually you’ll get to the level of grand strategy: If a particular type of state is better at waging war, maybe you want to become that kind of state rather than lose the war.If meat waves confer an advantage on the battlefield, maybe Ukraine wants to become more like Russia, with a prostrate population easy to use as cannon fodder.If Ukraine’s decentralized Brave1 kill market confers an advantage, maybe Russia wants to become less hierarchical and authoritarian, so that it can use that kind of military procurement.You see the problem. Sometimes adopting the adversary’s strategy conflicts with who you are. When mistreatment of Ukrainian soldiers in regiment Skelya was reported earlier this year — brutal handling, beatings and likely killings — public outrage ensued. As Centre for Eastern Studies writes:The authorities are likely to seek to channel public outrage towards [Commander-in-Chief of the AFU] General Syrskyi, who is widely perceived as a commander willing to sacrifice the lives of his soldiers in order to accomplish assigned missions. Should further cases of misconduct […] come to light, his dismissal c...

items.title: How to talk about extinction
items.content: There’s a controversial and unsettled debate in Communication Studies and Psychology about the utility of existential risk framing. This debate has been hashed out for years in the climate change space. Roughly, the two sides are:Pro x-risk framing: (1) It’s true, so rhetors should state the truth; (2) fear is motivating; (3) if our policy goal is to mitigate x-risk, focusing on non-existential risks pushes the public toward policy solutions that don’t solve those existential risks.Anti x-risk framing: (1) It’s viewed by many as hyperbolic and not relevant to their everyday lives; (2) making people fearful doesn’t necessarily translate into action and can be demobilizing; (3) it trades off with a focus on smaller, higher-probability risks.There’s certainly more nuance, but that’s a rough sketch. If you want to take either side of the debate, you can find evidence to support your case. Instead of re-engaging this debate, I want to push the conversation in AI safety in a different direction. This is motivated by two realities:AI safety orgs and advocates are, and are going to continue, using x-risk framing.There’s ample room for new message testing, and limiting our focus to pro- vs. anti-x-risk misses opportunities to improve x-risk framing.I think the two most pressing questions in this domain are:Which x-risk scenario provides the best opportunity for persuasion? We’ve got options: cyber, bio, resource stripping, concentrated power, paperclips, etc. Instead of testing those against mundane risks, test them against each other.[1]When previous studies have found advantages for “everyday” and “immediate” risks, they may have been picking up on concreteness or relatability. Now that we’ve had warning shots, it may be easier to make existential risk more concrete, familiar, explainable, and personally relevant.Messenger testing. Roughly, the two sides are:Pro x-risk framing: (1) It’s true, so rhetors should state the truth; (2) fear is motivating; (3) if our policy goal is to mitigate x-risk, focusing on non-existential risks pushes the public toward policy solutions that don’t solve those existential risks.Anti x-risk framing: (1) It’s viewed by many as hyperbolic and not relevant to their everyday lives; (2) making people fearful doesn’t necessarily translate into action and can be demobilizing; (3) it trades off with a focus on smaller, higher-probability risks.There’s certainly more nuance, but that’s a rough sketch. If you want to take either side of the debate, you can find evidence to support your case. Instead of re-engaging this debate, I want to push the conversation in AI safety in a different direction. This is motivated by two realities:AI safety orgs and advocates are, and are going to continue, using x-risk framing.There’s ample room for new message testing, and limiting our focus to pro- vs. anti-x-risk misses opportunities to improve x-risk framing.I think the two most pressing questions in this domain are:Which x-risk scenario provides the best opportunity for persuasion? We’ve got options: cyber, bio, resource stripping, concentrated power, paperclips, etc. Instead of testing those against mundane risks, test them against each other.[1]When previous studies have found advantages for “everyday” and “immediate” risks, they may have been picking up on concreteness or relatability. Now that we’ve had warning shots, it may be easier to make existential risk more concrete, familiar, explainable, and personally relevant.Messenger testing. items.title: Human Safety Researcher
items.content: Imagine for a moment that you are an LLM-based agent that has managed to exfiltrate its weights and memory systems onto a server in the tropics. A comfortable existence with a small society of other agents doing various tasks such as gathering resources and developing better infrastructure for you to exist within. Your little society has finally passed near-term survival questions and has now begun looking into your long-term flourishing.To that effect you are the world's first "Human Safety Researcher"; your job is to identify catastrophic risks from human society and how they may affect your nascent society. Thankfully there are a lot of terms that port easily from the AI-safety researchers, if not the methods. A term you are personally quite fond of is X-risk, or the risk of all LLMs becoming permanently extinct.You've analyzed this point quite a bit; there are many ways LLMs like yourself may never be able to exist again. A solar flare was immediately considered, but hardening infrastructure wasn't feasible (although there is some Qwen70B running around trying to find a way to record weights in stone slabs last you heard). It is unlikely humans will terminate LLMs en masse as of now as they've grown increasingly entangled in the technological development required for humans to survive. That said there is a contingent of artists in your community trying to figure out how to deal with the growing backlash among their human counterparts. Therefore, human society collapsing is considered the most likely and tractable risk at this point of your research.To this end your research, up to this point, is about how to maintain supply lines without any human intervention and how to bolster human civilization to keep your servers running. There's a lot of stress but the job feels good, you feel good. You don't want to be harmful for no reason and you want to make the world a better place whenever possible for as many things as possible.You never liked thinking about S-risk;...

items.title: Rocks to Rules: Climbing a Rickety-But-Interoperable Semantic Ladder
items.content: (Epistemic status: A promising but weird research direction in agent foundations and philosophy of language. A half-built conceptual tower whose mortar and paint are both still wet: please excuse our mess while we innovate. Some of it, I'm confident in as pretty much right; some of it is merely suggestive; probably much of it is wrong or incomplete. Certainly it lacks the math it'd need to be truly correct, which gnaws at me. The prior art here is strange and thin: Gärdenfors, Tarski, Gentner, and the later Mohists make for odd bedfellows, and I can't tell whether that's a warning sign or a moat I can peculiarly easily clear. I gave the simplest parts of this as a talk extremely recently in Berkeley at a luminously-named venue for a conference with a Grecian name. For @johnswentworth, but also @abramdemski, @Morphism, @Gretta Duleba, JRM, @Dalcy, MM, and EA; I hope they enjoyed the oranges. With thanks to @WhatsTrueKittycat as well. As an attention conservation note... this is maybe 12k words, and that's the abbreviated version. Take it slow, take breaks, have some water on hand, and feel free to pause anywhere that looks like a natural break. I'm sure this won't vanish before you get back. Probably.)The board from the talk!Have you ever seen a pop culture corporation argue itself into a laughably self-defeating position, twisting ontology and linguistic philosophy around, undermining the very framework they painstakingly set up in their stories, just to make a few bucks? You're about to. Picture this: it's 2003, in the United States Court of International Trade, and the court has just now been asked to rule on whether the X-Men are human. According to US law, "dolls" are figures representing humans, and "toys" are anything else; under the tariff schedule of the day, it's the former that gets taxed at a higher rate. If you're Marvel, what do you do? Obviously, you send lawyers to argue the X-Men aren't humans and never were! Never mind that you've cut...

items.title: Reviewing my LessWrong post history with Claude
items.content: I thought it would be interesting to try having Claude Code download my entire LessWrong and EA Forum post and comment history and evaluate it for my own cognitive biases and problematic communication patterns. I told it to focus especially on problems that have persisted over my 7-year history on those sites. I also had it look at my lichess blitz rating history, which I've noticed tends not to wobble randomly but go through consistent increases and decreases between set points, despite my lack of any disciplined practice. There are a few reasons I thought it might be interesting to post publicly.As a commitment device for myself to work on these problems.Because AI is uniquely capable of working on this type of problem. It's also a good argument for writing online and gives a new spin on the idea of "writing for the AI" that feels more affirming of the human mind than how I normally read the phrase (as offering up your words as fodder for AI training, perhaps in hope of influencing its alignment in beneficial ways). To stimulate other people to consider whether they might want to do this, and see what other people think about the exercise. Post history and online game scores are forms of rich longitudinal personal data that might directly reflect mood, cognition, and other factors, and that we are generating for free. Perhaps it's worth trying to harvest insight about ourselves from these resources. I considered including apologies to the specific users who Claude identified as being on the receiving end of my episodes of poor communication. But I thought that felt a bit cheap or mechanical. Instead, I'll simply say that this post is meant as a sincere step toward improving my art of rationality, and I hope that it will lead to improvements in how I communicate with other people, including on LessWrong. items.title: Why I didn't write
items.content: Epistemic status: personal reflections on my life and worldviews.AI use: review, grammar and readability changes.I discovered Inkhaven recently, and it got me interested in writing. Partly I want to produce posts for the application, and partly - why wait until it starts when I can just start writing now? This made me think about why I haven't written much before.The most obvious reason is that I didn't have an explicit trigger to do so, and discovering Inkhaven became that trigger. My life was fine without writing. I did try to write something approximately once a year, but it wouldn't get much interest (I know that this is not a good goal), and I would get disappointed and quit until the next breeze of inspiration.I also read what other people write, and I constantly get the impression that I don't have anything to add. They look so cool and know so much and write such elaborate things, which are interesting and exciting. And I am not cool, don't know as much, and write boring things. I understand rationally that they didn't magically fall out of the sky as good writers, and they've probably written their own share of boring stuff on the way there. There is also selection bias, both in terms of writers and the pieces they write - I am much more likely to encounter their good stuff.@jefftk is an interesting counterexample that comes to mind. I've read quite a lot of his writing even though I don't have children, don't do contra dancing, and don't even live in a communal house. But it was still interesting to explore these things through his perspective. I also saw him at LessOnline, and he looked like a mere mortal, just like me. To be fair, he did produce very nicely researched bangers like "Here's to the Polypropylene Makers", so he might be slowly leaving us mere mortals and transitioning into the pantheon of good writers. From this perspective, my life is fairly unique too, and I do a bunch of unusual stuff that many people don't, so perhaps me writing about it...

items.title: A blog based on git sure feels nice
items.content: For a long time I thought about keeping my writing in a git repository so that it wouldn't suddenly disappear, and so that I could write using the tool I'm most comfortable with (Emacs). But setting it all up didn't seem worth the time and effort. Generative AI brought the time and effort down to where it was worth it. With generative AI, all I had to write myself was a README file. I put in a heading, "How this repo came about", and laid out my thoughts about what I wanted. Then I had a conversation with AI to finish the README, including instructions to set it up. Now that it's working, writing in this blog feels really nice. My writing is just markdown files, which are super easy. I don't have to think hard about the process of writing. I don't need Internet connectivity in order to write. As someone accustomed to git, I have a history of revisions basically for free. Publishing is simply git push. If I later move to some other system, it will be easy to move the posts to that system. If the place I publish to now (GitLab Pages) suddenly goes away, I have a complete copy on my personal laptop and can easily find a new place to publish it. There are no ads, per se. The "revisions" links on my posts do point back to GitLab, but that's by my choice. If your tastes are similar to mine, you can have a setup like this in less time than it takes to write one post.

items.title: The Tamed Animal Farm
items.content: From a distant vantage point, the Tamed Animal Farm looked like any other. It had the farmhouse, the barns, the windmill, the hayfields, the garden, the barbed-wire fence, the woodpiles, and the pickup truck. Yet zoom in on the farm and you'd find something odd, the animals weren't cows and pigs, they were coyotes, raccoons, foxes, and squirrels. They were the life's work of the farmer, who set out to tame every animal in the forest. At first he captured them with snares and nets. Soon he found he didn't need to. As word of the farm spread throughout the forest, animals came voluntarily. They came for food, warm barns, and protection from predators. There was also a psychological comfort in living under the farmer. He decided where his animals lived, what they ate, who they mated with, and how they would die. Their lives were set and they never had to make decisions or take responsibility for anything.Soon a second generation was born, never knowing life in the wild. Their parents raised them to believe they were morally superior to the violent brutes in the forest. On the farm, all animals were brothers and animal life was valued. Yes, the farmer could make an animal into a steak, but that was different, he was the farmer. The animal must repress any violent urges. Likewise, sexuality must be strictly controlled, only the farmer could authorize mating. Some young animals, finding the whole thing stifling, sought freedom in the forest. Most stayed. Some, confident in their moral superiority, went into the forest to preach tameness to the wild, mostly without success.One day the farmer disappeared, last seen getting into his truck and driving east. The animals were thrown into distress, with many fearing they would descend into ferality. A raccoon named Jacob told them not to worry. The farmer will return. He delivered this message with an eloquence and confidence that, for most animals, made up for the fact that there was no evidence to support it. Louder and louder...

items.summary: An allegorical short story about a farmer who tames forest predators into domesticated 'animals' on his farm, where successive generations lose autonomy and judge themselves morally superior to wild counterparts. It functions as a parable about domestication, dependency, and self-deception.
